## Lab Thirteen Work

Suppose that you’ve been given raw registration data for a university event. Students entered their contact info in inconsistent ways, and your job is to clean and extract usable information. The code chunk below creates a tibble of 15 of these registrations. 

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(stringr)

registrations <- tibble(
  id = 1:15,
  contact_info = c(
    "John Doe, johndoe@gmail.com, 608-555-1234",
    "Jane Smith | (608) 555 9876 | jane_smith@outlook.com",
    "Bob: bob123@yahoo.com",
    "Call me at 608.555.0000 - Mike",
    "Sarah (sarah@school.edu)",
    "No contact info provided",
    "Reach me: student@@college..edu",
    "Alex - 6085554321 - alex99@gmail.com",
    "Chris: chris.p.bacon@uni.edu, phone: (608)555-2222",
    "Email only: cool_student@college.org",
    "Phone only: 608 555 9999",
    "Emergency contact: mom 715-555-1212",
    "Contact: invalid_email@.com",
    "Best way: text 608-555-ABCD",
    "Alternate: first.last@company.co.uk"
  )
)
```


1. Which rows contain \emph{valid-looking} email addresses?
```{r}
email_regex <- "[A-Za-z_.]+[0-9]*@[A-Za-z]+.[a-z]+"
str_view_all(registrations$contact_info, email_regex)
valid_emails <- str_extract_all(registrations$contact_info, email_regex)
```

2. Create a new column in the `registrations` tibble containing the email addresses.
```{r}
registrations <- registrations %>%
  mutate(email_adresses = valid_emails)
```

3. Clean and standardize the email addresses in the new column.
```{r}

```

4. Which rows contain phone numbers?
```{r}
phones_regx <- "\\(?[0-9]{3}[\\)-.\\s]{0,2}[0-9]{3}[\\)-.\\s]{0,2}[0-9A-Z]{4}"
str_view_all(registrations$contact_info, phones_regx)
valid_phones <- str_extract_all(registrations$contact_info, phones_regx)
```

5. Create a new column in the `registrations` tibble containing the phone numbers.
```{r}
registrations <- registrations %>%
  mutate(phone_numbers = valid_phones)
```

6. Clean and standardize the phone numbers in the new column.
```{r}
registrations <- registrations %>%
  mutate(phone_numbers = str_replace_all(phone_numbers, "[^0-9A-Z]", ""), phone_numbers = str_replace(phone_numbers, "([0-9]{3})([0-9]{3})([0-9A-Z]{4})", "(\\1) \\2-\\3"))
```

7. Flag suspicious registrations (with a new column). These should have no phone AND no email address, or are otherwise clearly bad patterns.
```{r}
registrations <- registrations %>%
  mutate(suspicious = !(str_detect(phone_numbers, phones_regx) | str_detect(email_adresses, email_regex)))
```


## Lab Fourteen Work

Project Gutenberg is a digital archive of public domain books. The R package `gutenbergr` facilitates the importation of these texts into R.

You can see the books that are available with `gutenberg_metadata`
```{r}
library(gutenbergr)
library(tidytext)
library(textdata)
library(tidyverse)
```

1. Use `str_detect` to find the ID of the novel Pride and Prejudice.
```{r}
which(str_detect(gutenberg_metadata$title, "Pride and Prejudice"))
```

2. We notice that there are several versions. The `gutenberg_works()` function filters this table to remove replicates and include only English language works. Read the help file and use this function to find the ID for Pride and Prejudice.
```{r}
gutenberg_works(title == "Pride and Prejudice")
```

3. Use the `gutenberg_download` function to download the text for Pride and Prejudice. Save it to an object called book.
```{r}
book <- gutenberg_download(gutenberg_id = "1342")
```

4. Add two variables to this `book` object: line numbers and page numbers. For pages, you can assume that there are 80 lines per page.
```{r}
book <- book %>% 
  mutate(line_numbers = 1:length(book$text)) %>%
  mutate(page_numbers = (line_numbers %/% 80) + 1)
```

5. Use the `tidytext` package to create a tidy table with all the words in the text. Save the table in an object called `book_words`
```{r}
book_words <- book %>%
  select(line_numbers, page_numbers, text) %>%  
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%               
  select(line_numbers, page_numbers, word) 
```

6. Add a variable to this `book_words` object giving the index of the word. 
```{r}
book_words <- book_words %>%
  mutate(index = 1:length(word))
```

7. Remove the stop words and numbers from the words object. 
```{r}
book_words <- book_words %>%
  filter(!word %in% stop_words$word)
```

8. Now use the AFINN lexicon to assign a sentiment value to each word.
```{r}
afinn <- get_sentiments("afinn")
book_words <- book_words %>% 
  inner_join(afinn, by = "word")
```

9. Make a plot of sentiment score versus location in the book and add a smoother.
```{r}
sentiment_by_page <- book_words %>%
  group_by(page_numbers) %>%
  summarize(sentiment = sum(value))

sentiment_plt <- ggplot(sentiment_by_page, aes(x = page_numbers, y = sentiment)) 
sentiment_plt + geom_line() + geom_smooth(se = FALSE) + labs(title = "Sentiment Over Pride and Prejudice", x = "Page Number", y = "Sentiment Score")


```

10. Plot that average score by page. Add a smoother that appears to go through data. (NOTE: the lab file had information about 300 words per page -- you can still use this if you want, or you can use the page numbers already created.)
```{r}
sentiment_by_page_2 <- book_words %>%
  group_by(page_numbers) %>%
  summarize(avg_sentiment = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE))

sentiment_plt_2 <- ggplot(sentiment_by_page_2, aes(x = page_numbers, y = avg_sentiment)) 
sentiment_plt_2 + geom_line(color = "blue") + geom_smooth(se = FALSE, method = "loess", span = 0.2, color = "red") + labs(title = "Average Sentiment Over Pride and Prejudice", x = "Page Number", y = "Average Sentiment Score")
```

11. Make a similar plot, but looking at average score by chapter. (How can you identify chapters? Hint: a regular expression?) 
```{r}
chapter_info <- book %>%
  mutate(chapter_name = str_extract(text, regex("^CHAPTER\\s+\\w+", ignore_case = TRUE))) %>%
  fill(chapter_name) %>%                    
  mutate(chapter_num = as.integer(factor(chapter_name))) %>%  
  select(line_numbers, chapter_num)

book_words <- book_words %>%
  left_join(chapter_info, by = "line_numbers")

sentiment_by_chapter <- book_words %>%
  group_by(chapter_num) %>%
  summarize(avg_sentiment = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot(sentiment_by_chapter, aes(x = chapter_num, y = avg_sentiment)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, method = "loess", span = 0.3, color = "darkred") +
  labs(
    title = "Average Sentiment by Chapter in Pride and Prejudice",
    x = "Chapter",
    y = "Average Sentiment Score"
  )


```
